To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the HLA-B*5701, -B*57-01 and -B*57:02 alleles are associated with the most strikingly protective effects against HIV disease, that the HCP5 and ZNRD loci are associated with HIV disease, but that these associations are largely attributable to the strong LD between these genes and the HLA-A10 and HLA-B alleles, and that the strong protective effects of the B*57 alleles are independent of their impact on viral replication.
the HIV-1 disease-influencing effects associated with ZNRD, HCP5, and HLA-C allelic polymorphisms are attributable mainly to either HLA-A10-containing haplotypes or HLA-B57-containing haplotopes.

the disease-influencing effects of ZNRD, HCP5, and HLA-C polymorphisms are mainly attributable to either HLA-A10 and/or HLA-B*5701, and that the protective effects of HLA-B57 alleles on AIDS progression rates are independent of their strong influence on viral control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis for HIV/AIDS.
the genetic factors that influence disease progression and viral replication.
the role of genetic polymorphisms in influencing HIV-1 disease progression and viral load.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV-1 disease-influencing effects associated with ZNRD, HCP5, and HLA-C are mainly attributable to the HLA-B*5701 and/or HLA-B*5801 alleles.

ZNRD1 polymorphisms influence HIV disease in European Americans mainly through their association with HLA-A10-containing haplotypes and that the HCP5 and C alleles exert disease-influencing effects mainly through HLA-B*5701 and HLA-B57-containing haplotopes.
the HCP5 and ZNRD polymorphisms are associated with HIV viral control, but the effects of these polymorphisms are dependent on HLA class I alleles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the HIV-1 disease-influencing effects associated with ZNRD and HCP5 are largely attributable to HLA class I alleles, and that these alleles, in combination with HLA-C and B*57, stratify HIV-1-inflicted damage into those that are either strikingly retarded or accelerated.

HLA-C and/or HCP5 alleles, in the absence of HLA-B57, are not protective against HIV disease, but in the presence of B57 are associated with either striking protection or accelerated disease, respectively.
HLA-A10 and HLA-B57-containing alleles are the major HIV-1 disease-influencing alleles, and the HCP5 and C alleles are secondary to them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of the HLA-C and the ZNRD genes on viral control and disease progression are mediated by HLA-A10 and HLA-B57, respectively, and that the HCP5 and the HLA-C genes are linked to HLA-B57.
HCP5-G and ZNRD2-A10 alleles are associated with a slower HIV disease progression and lower viral loads in HIV-1-inflected individuals.
the effects of HLA-C and/or ZNRD1 on HIV-1 disease are mainly attributable to either the presence of HLA-A10 and/or the absence of HLA-C alleles that are associated with progressive disease.
